issues.legal_issue: An ancient Hindu adoption may be proved, despite the absence of direct evidence of the giving-and-taking ceremony, through long and consistent recognition supported by the surrounding evidence, and may be treated as valid where no evidence shows it was invalid.
material_facts: The alleged adoption had occurred about 54 years before the suit, and the passage of time made direct oral evidence difficult to obtain.
The alleged adoptive father consistently treated the claimant as his son in documents and testimony over many years, including school, court, and income-tax records.

Relatives and other persons, including the natural-succession claimant, treated the alleged adopted son as the adoptive father's son both during the adoptive father's life and afterward, before the dispute arose.

Witnesses testified to circumstances indicating that the child had been taken into the adoptive family soon after birth, although satisfactory direct evidence of the actual adoption ceremony was not produced.

The alleged adopted son and others acted on the basis of the claimed relationship in business and property matters; the contrary description of him as the natural father's son appeared in only one decree and was outweighed by the other evidence.
The alleged adopter's family had lost several children before the alleged adoption, and the court found no evidence that the adoption was invalid.
issues.conclusion: The alleged adoption was proved and was valid. The long, consistent recognition and the other evidence supported the inference that the adoption had occurred, and there was no evidence showing it to be invalid.
issues.legal_principle: A person alleging adoption to displace natural succession bears the burden of proving the factum and validity of the adoption. Under Hindu law, a valid adoption requires a formal giving and taking, including actual delivery and receipt of the child, though no particular form is prescribed. In an ancient adoption, the absence of direct evidence must be assessed in light of the passage of time; long recognition by the adoptive family and conduct and documents founded on the relationship may support the inference of adoption and attract a strong presumption in its favour. Once the court is satisfied that the adoption occurred, validity may be inferred in the absence of evidence to the contrary. The court applied Addagada Raghavamma v. Addagada Chenchamma and Lakshman Singh Kothari v. Smt. Rup Kanwar; it approved Rajendrao Nath Holder v. Jogendro Nath Banerjee and relied also on Rup Narain v. Mst. Gopal Devi and Balinki Padhano v. Gopalkrishna Padhano.

rule.if: property_succession_dispute and ancient_adoption_claim and long_adoptive_parent_recognition and long_family_recognition and corroborating_circumstances and not evidence_of_invalidity

predicates.property_succession_dispute: One person sought property through natural succession while another asserted status as an adopted child of the property holder.
predicates.ancient_adoption_claim: The claimed adoption occurred so long before the dispute that direct witnesses or other direct proof were difficult to obtain.
predicates.long_adoptive_parent_recognition: The alleged adoptive parent repeatedly treated the claimant as a child in statements, documents, or conduct before the dispute arose.
predicates.long_family_recognition: Relatives or other persons connected with the family, including a person later disputing the adoption, treated the claimant as the alleged adoptive parent's child over a substantial period before the controversy.
predicates.corroborating_circumstances: Other evidence, such as testimony, conduct, possession, or documents made on the basis of the claimed relationship, supported the alleged adoption.
predicates.evidence_of_invalidity: Evidence showed that the alleged adoption was invalid.

issues.definition: When a property succession dispute involves a remote adoption claim, sustained recognition by the alleged adoptive parent and family, corroborating circumstances, and no evidence of invalidity mean the adoption is proved and valid.
